rules: Title plans and registers record the general position of boundaries unless a boundary is determined as exact.
An index polygon is an index showing the indicative location of a registered title rather than an exact legal extent.
The title plan and register share the title number identifier.
Every registered title has at least one index polygon.
Each index polygon has a unique polygon identifier managed through dataset lifecycle rules.
The relationship between a registered title and one or more polygons is managed through the title number.
INSPIRE polygons are a subset of the National Polygon Dataset with simpler identifier, creation-date and update-date attributes.
Gaps, overlaps, slivers and underlaps exist in the polygon dataset and some are genuine.
Small technical polygon overlaps can arise from mapping inconsistencies and do not necessarily represent a real title conflict.
An index polygon may be the same size, larger or smaller than the title-plan extent and must not be relied upon as exact.

The Planning Data API exposes more than 100 planning and housing datasets through a consistent interface.
Entity search supports JSON, HTML and GeoJSON response extensions.
The organisation_entity parameter filters entities managed by specified organisations.
The curie parameter accepts an array of CURIE identifiers.
The prefix parameter accepts an array of entity prefixes.
The period parameter controls whether current or all entries are included.
The quality parameter filters entities by quality classification.
The geometry_reference parameter applies spatial relations using geometries of entities with supplied references.
The geometry_curie parameter applies spatial relations using geometries of entities matching supplied CURIEs.

Each ground-truth point is specified with plus or minus 3 centimetres RMSE accuracy.
Ground-truth points are collected on flat unambiguous surfaces using GPS.
A ground-truth survey may support multiple LiDAR surveys if it is under five years old, or under three years for coastal projects.
LiDAR surveys must report absolute error below plus or minus 15 centimetres RMSE to pass quality control.
LiDAR surveys must report standard deviation and random error below 10 centimetres to pass quality control.
The Environment Agency expects relative height error to be no more than plus or minus 5 centimetres.
A one-metre DSM survey point cloud has an average density of at least one point per square metre.
A fifty-centimetre DSM requires an average point density of four points per square metre.
A twenty-five-centimetre DSM requires an average point density of sixteen points per square metre.
Point-density figures apply to the DSM; under vegetation the DTM may not reach one point per square metre and the source point cloud is not a regular grid.
